notes: Nine independent higher-demand AQA-style Amount of Substance questions; original practice, not copied or verified published AQA questions. All solutions are for marking after an attempt.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Amount of Substance practice
questions.prompt: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its measured relative molecular mass is 180. Calculate the empirical formula and molecular formula. Explain why the percentages can be treated as masses in grams and why the empirical formula alone is insufficient to identify the molecular formula. Relative atomic masses C=12.0, H=1.0, O=16.0.
markPoints: Assume a 100 g sample, giving masses 40.0 g C, 6.7 g H and 53.3 g O.
Divide each amount by the smallest to obtain the approximate ratio C:H:O=1:2:1.
The molecular multiplier is 180/30=6, giving molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆.
The empirical formula supplies only relative numbers of atoms, so an independently determined relative molecular mass is needed.
questions.modelAnswer: Assume a 100 g sample, giving masses 40.0 g C, 6.7 g H and 53.3 g O. Convert masses to moles: C=40.0/12=3.333, H=6.7/1=6.7, O=53.3/16=3.331. Divide each amount by the smallest to obtain the approximate ratio C:H:O=1:2:1. The empirical formula is CH₂O. The empirical formula mass is 12+2+16=30. The molecular multiplier is 180/30=6, giving molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆. The empirical formula supplies only relative numbers of atoms, so an independently determined relative molecular mass is needed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Amount of Substance practice
questions.prompt: A volatile substance is vaporised. The gas sample has a mass of 0.250 g and occupies 145 cm³ at 373 K and 100 kPa. Using pV=nRT with R=8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, calculate the amount of gas and its molar mass. Explain why converting cm³ directly into dm³ is not sufficient when using SI units in pV=nRT.
markPoints: Convert 145 cm³ to 1.45×10⁻⁴ m³ by dividing by 10⁶.
The ideal gas equation expects volume in m³, not dm³, for the SI form with R=8.31.
A suitable answer states SI units and uses consistent significant figures.
questions.modelAnswer: Convert pressure 100 kPa to 100000 Pa. Convert 145 cm³ to 1.45×10⁻⁴ m³ by dividing by 10⁶. Use n=pV/(RT). Substitute n=(100000×1.45×10⁻⁴)/(8.31×373)≈4.68×10⁻³ mol. Calculate M=m/n=0.250/0.00468≈53.4 g mol⁻¹. The ideal gas equation expects volume in m³, not dm³, for the SI form with R=8.31. A suitable answer states SI units and uses consistent significant figures.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Amount of Substance practice
questions.prompt: 2.43 g Mg reacts with 100.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl: Mg+2HCl→MgCl₂+H₂. (a) Find moles of each reactant. (b) Identify the limiting reagent. (c) Find hydrogen moles and approximate hydrogen volume at RTP (24 dm³ mol⁻¹). (d) Determine the mass of magnesium left over. Ar(Mg)=24.3.
markPoints: Mg:HCl reacting ratio is 1:2, so HCl is limiting even though initial moles are equal.
questions.modelAnswer: Moles Mg=2.43/24.3=0.100 mol. Moles HCl=1.00×(100/1000)=0.100 mol. Mg:HCl reacting ratio is 1:2, so HCl is limiting even though initial moles are equal. Moles Mg consumed =0.100/2=0.0500 mol. Moles H₂ produced =0.0500 mol. Gas volume at RTP≈0.0500×24=1.20 dm³. Moles Mg remaining=0.100−0.0500=0.0500 mol. Mass Mg remaining=0.0500×24.3≈1.22 g.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Amount of Substance practice
questions.prompt: Ethene is prepared from ethanol by C₂H₅OH→C₂H₄+H₂O. When 9.20 g ethanol reacts, 4.76 g ethene is obtained. (a) Calculate the theoretical ethene mass. (b) Determine percentage yield. (c) Calculate percentage atom economy for ethene. (d) Explain why percentage yield and atom economy are different. Mr ethanol=46.0, ethene=28.0, water=18.0.
markPoints: Stoichiometry 1:1 gives theoretical ethene moles=0.200 mol.
Atom economy predicts how reactant atoms distribute into desired product and by-products.
Percentage yield compares measured product with the stoichiometric maximum and depends on reaction efficiency/recovery.
questions.modelAnswer: Moles ethanol=9.20/46.0=0.200 mol. Stoichiometry 1:1 gives theoretical ethene moles=0.200 mol. Theoretical ethene mass=0.200×28.0=5.60 g. Percentage yield=(4.76/5.60)×100=85.0%. Atom economy for ethene=(28.0/46.0)×100≈60.9%. Atom economy predicts how reactant atoms distribute into desired product and by-products. Percentage yield compares measured product with the stoichiometric maximum and depends on reaction efficiency/recovery.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Amount of Substance practice
questions.prompt: A 4.92 g sample of magnesium sulfate hydrate MgSO₄·xH₂O is heated until its final anhydrous solid mass is 2.40 g. Assume the lost mass is entirely water and no MgSO₄ decomposes. Determine x and explain the purpose of repeatedly checking for constant mass. Ar Mg=24.3, S=32.1, O=16.0, H=1.0.
markPoints: Formula is MgSO₄·7H₂O; constant mass supports complete release of removable water.
questions.modelAnswer: Mass of water lost=4.92−2.40=2.52 g. Molar mass MgSO₄=24.3+32.1+4×16.0=120.4 g mol⁻¹. Moles MgSO₄=2.40/120.4≈0.01993 mol. Moles H₂O=2.52/18.0=0.140 mol. Ratio water:salt=0.140/0.01993≈7.02:1, which rounds to 7:1. Formula is MgSO₄·7H₂O; constant mass supports complete release of removable water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Amount of Substance practice
questions.prompt: A solution of barium chloride is mixed with sodium sulfate solution; insoluble barium sulfate forms. (a) Write a balanced full equation with state symbols. (b) Write the complete ionic equation. (c) Identify spectator ions and give the net ionic equation. (d) Explain why spectator ions are omitted.
markPoints: Aqueous ionic reactants split into Ba²⁺, 2Cl⁻, 2Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻.
Product side has BaSO₄(s) plus 2Na⁺(aq) and 2Cl⁻(aq).
Spectator ions are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ because they appear unchanged on both sides.
The net ionic equation keeps only the species changed by the reaction and balances charge and atoms.
questions.modelAnswer: Full equation: BaCl₂(aq)+Na₂SO₄(aq)→BaSO₄(s)+2NaCl(aq). Aqueous ionic reactants split into Ba²⁺, 2Cl⁻, 2Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻. Product side has BaSO₄(s) plus 2Na⁺(aq) and 2Cl⁻(aq). Spectator ions are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ because they appear unchanged on both sides. Net ionic equation: Ba²⁺(aq)+SO₄²⁻(aq)→BaSO₄(s). The net ionic equation keeps only the species changed by the reaction and balances charge and atoms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Amount of Substance practice
questions.prompt: In an acid–alkali titration, 25.0 cm³ of an unknown NaOH solution reacts 1:1 with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl. Titre readings (cm³) are 23.40, 23.45, 24.70 and 23.50. (a) Select concordant data and calculate mean titre. (b) Find the NaOH concentration. (c) If each burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³, determine the absolute and percentage uncertainty in the mean titre considered as a difference of two readings. (d) Explain why a pipette is rinsed with solution and the burette with titrant.
markPoints: Exclude 24.70 cm³ as an outlier relative to the three close readings.
The HCl:NaOH ratio is 1:1, so n(NaOH)=0.002345 mol.
Each titre uses two readings, so absolute titre uncertainty is ±(0.05+0.05)=±0.10 cm³.
Rinsing calibrated apparatus with the intended solution avoids unplanned dilution by residual water.
questions.modelAnswer: Exclude 24.70 cm³ as an outlier relative to the three close readings. Mean titre=(23.40+23.45+23.50)/3=23.45 cm³. Use n(HCl)=0.100×0.02345=0.002345 mol. The HCl:NaOH ratio is 1:1, so n(NaOH)=0.002345 mol. Concentration NaOH=0.002345/0.0250=0.0938 mol dm⁻³. Each titre uses two readings, so absolute titre uncertainty is ±(0.05+0.05)=±0.10 cm³. Percentage titre uncertainty=(0.10/23.45)×100≈0.426%. Rinsing calibrated apparatus with the intended solution avoids unplanned dilution by residual water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Amount of Substance practice
questions.prompt: A 2.00 g impure calcium carbonate sample reacts with excess 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl. The resulting mixture, after reaction and suitable preparation, is made up to 250.0 cm³. A 25.0 cm³ aliquot of the acidic solution needs 18.60 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH for neutralisation. Non-carbonate impurities are inert. Calculate the percentage by mass of CaCO₃ in the original sample, explaining why the aliquot and CaCO₃:HCl mole ratios matter. Mr(CaCO₃)=100.1. The reaction is CaCO₃+2HCl→CaCl₂+CO₂+H₂O.
markPoints: Moles NaOH used with aliquot=0.100×0.01860=0.001860 mol.
Neutralisation is 1:1, so 0.001860 mol HCl remains in the 25.0 cm³ aliquot.
Total diluted volume is 250.0 cm³, ten times the aliquot, so total HCl remaining=0.01860 mol.
questions.modelAnswer: Initial moles HCl=1.00×0.0500=0.0500 mol. Moles NaOH used with aliquot=0.100×0.01860=0.001860 mol. Neutralisation is 1:1, so 0.001860 mol HCl remains in the 25.0 cm³ aliquot. Total diluted volume is 250.0 cm³, ten times the aliquot, so total HCl remaining=0.01860 mol. Acid consumed by carbonate=0.0500−0.01860=0.03140 mol. CaCO₃:HCl ratio 1:2 gives n(CaCO₃)=0.03140/2=0.01570 mol. Mass CaCO₃=0.01570×100.1≈1.572 g. Percentage CaCO₃=1.572/2.00×100≈78.6%.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Amount of Substance practice
questions.prompt: A solution contains 0.0200 mol CaCl₂, assumed to dissociate completely. (a) Find moles of chloride ions and total ions. (b) Calculate the number of chloride ions and the total number of ions using Nₐ=6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹. (c) Explain why the total number of dissolved ions is three times the number of CaCl₂ formula units.
markPoints: CaCl₂ dissociates into one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻ ions per formula unit.
The calcium-to-chloride ion ratio is 1:2, giving three ions per formula unit.
questions.modelAnswer: CaCl₂ dissociates into one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻ ions per formula unit. Chloride ion amount=2×0.0200=0.0400 mol. Total ion amount=3×0.0200=0.0600 mol. Number of chloride ions=0.0400×6.02×10²³≈2.41×10²². Total number of ions=0.0600×6.02×10²³≈3.61×10²². The calcium-to-chloride ion ratio is 1:2, giving three ions per formula unit.
